summary.text: 动 is the simplified form of 動, a character for acting and moving. In the received traditional form, 力 contributes meaning and 重 serves as a likely sound component; reconstructions compare 動 with 重 in its ‘heavy’ reading.

formation.text: The received form 動 is phonosemantic: 力 contributes meaning associated with strength and action, while 重 provides a sound cue. This analysis applies to the received form; the reported bronze-script graph does not establish that these parts were already present there.

components.text: In received 動, 力 contributes the meaning of strength or action. Whether it was already a separate component in the reported bronze graph is uncertain.

In received 動, 重 is the phonetic component. The sound comparison uses its ‘heavy’ reading; an interpretation of early 重 as a person bearing a load does not establish the object’s name or pronunciation.

sound_limitation.text: The comparison concerns 動 and 重 in its ‘heavy’ reading; it does not establish the name or pronunciation of the object interpreted as a load in early forms of 重.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, 動 *[Cə-ә m-]tˤoŋʔ and 重 *N-t<r>oŋʔ in its ‘heavy’ reading are similar, supporting a likely phonetic relationship. That system gives 重 ‘repeat’ a distinct reconstruction; the comparison was not independently reverified in the recorded research.

history.text: A paleographic account identifies a bronze-script graph catalogued as 童 with 動. The curated bronze-style rendering shows this candidate graph. Its identification, original referent, and connection to the received form remain uncertain; no direct sequence is established.

The received form’s analysis as 力 plus phonetic 重 is transmitted in the seal-script tradition. The curated seal-style rendering illustrates that analysis, not a proven transition from the bronze-style graph.
In 1956, 动 was standardized as the simplified form paired with 動. How the cloud-like portion acquired its present shape is unresolved.
An old form 𨔝 is recorded with 辵. Its graphic connection to 动 is not established.

uncertainties.text: No oracle-bone form or absolute date for the earliest graph is given. The reported bronze-script identification, the early graph’s referent, and its connection to the received form remain uncertain.
Early forms of 重 have been interpreted as a person bearing a bag or load, but the object’s identity and spoken name are not established. This does not decide 重’s phonetic role in received 動.

senses.text: The transmitted gloss 作也 means ‘act’ or ‘do.’ Cited textual and manuscript examples also show action or movement, but are not dated precisely enough here to order them.
A cited Mawangdui manuscript example uses 動 for changing position or state. Its development in relation to the action sense is unresolved.
Modern records include ‘move’ and ‘happen,’ as well as the nouns ‘movement’ and ‘action.’ The evidence does not establish a single chronological path among these meanings.

developments.text: Both uses are attested, but their transition and direction are unresolved.

limitations.text: The cited textual and manuscript passages do not provide absolute dates sufficient to establish the chronology of these senses.
The early bronze graph’s meaning and its semantic path to ‘act’ or ‘move’ remain unresolved.

overview.text: 动 means ‘act’ or ‘move’ and is the simplified form of 動. In traditional 動, 力 contributes meaning and 重 likely signals sound through its ‘heavy’ reading, which had a similar Old Chinese reconstruction to 動.

components.text: In traditional 動, 力 links the character with strength and action.
In traditional 動, 重 likely signals sound through its ‘heavy’ reading; this does not establish the name or pronunciation of the load interpreted in early forms of 重.

Etymological analysis: 重 (phonetic)

The database records bronze-script 童 and 動 as the same graph, and describes the small-seal 動 as a phonosemantic character with 力 as semantic element and 重 as phonetic. This supports the received character analysis but does not establish the identity of the earliest bronze graph’s original referent.
evidence.title: 漢字「動」：字形演變

evidence.source: Hong Kong Chinese University, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 動 as 力 plus phonetic 重 and gives its basic sense as action/movement. It cites the received Shuowen explanation and early textual examples: 《易·繫辭上》 “擬之而後言，議之而後動” and Mawangdui 《合陰陽》 slip 111 “觀八動”. It also cites Mawangdui 《十問》 slip 16 for “能動其形,” a use meaning to change position or state. These attestations distinguish the early action sense from a later documented change-of-state use; the cited page does not give absolute dates for the texts or slips.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「動」

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcription of Shuowen and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The entry transmits 許慎’s gloss “作也。从力重聲” (“to act/do; from 力, with 重 as phonetic”) and records 𨔝 as an old-form 動 written with 辵. Duan Yucai glosses 作 as 起 (“arise/begin”). This is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of the graph’s pre-seal history.
evidence.title: 說文解字「動」

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary indexes 動 as the standard form and records Mandarin dòng; it transmits the Shuowen analysis and the old form 𨔝 from 辵. This record supports the traditional graph’s lexicographic account; it does not give an ancestry relation between 动 and an ancient component shape.
evidence.title: [A00395] 動 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction data, version 1.1
evidence.text: In this reconstruction system, 動 ‘move’ is Middle Chinese duwngX and Old Chinese *[Cə-ә m-]tˤoŋʔ; 重 zhòng ‘heavy’ is reconstructed *N-t<r>oŋʔ, while 重 chóng ‘repeat; double’ has a distinct reconstruction *[m]-troŋ. The forms support a historical phonetic relationship in the relevant reading, while showing that 重 has multiple readings and the matching is not a simple identity in every sense.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction data, version 1.1
evidence.text: 重 zhòng ‘heavy’ is listed with Middle Chinese drjowngX and Old Chinese *N-t<r>oŋʔ; 重 chóng ‘repeat; double’ is *[m]-troŋ. This is the same reconstruction system and variant scope used for the 動 comparison.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

evidence.text: The database asserts that bronze-script 童 and 動 were the same graph and that later small-seal 動 has 力 as semantic and 重 as phonetic. This does not establish that 力 was already a separate semantic component in the bronze graph, nor that 童 was historically replaced by 重. The component relationship between bronze 童 and later 重 is therefore uncertain as a historical ancestor claim; it should not be inferred just from similar forms or sound.
evidence.title: 漢字「動」：字形演變

evidence.source: Hong Kong Chinese University, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes early oracle-bone and bronze forms of 重 as 人 plus 東, with 東 interpreted as a bag or sack, depicting a person bearing a load; it gives ‘heavy’ as the basic sense and says 東 also contributes sound. This is the source’s analysis of 重’s own graphic history. The independently established phonetic role of 重 in 動 does not depend on proving the depicted load’s name or pronunciation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「重」

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction data, version 1.1

This phonological comparison supports 重’s sound role in the later compound under Baxter–Sagart’s system, but does not independently establish the name of any pictured object in 重’s early forms.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.

search_audit.query: 1956 汉字简化方案 动（動）
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the scheme reproduction, including its resolution date, effective date for the first table, and 动（動） entry.

gaps: No visually inspected glyph images in this research; conclusions rely on source descriptions and the Academia Sinica record.

The inspected sources did not establish an oracle-bone attestation of 動. The Academia Sinica page locates a bronze form under collection no. 集成02841 but the early graph’s original referent and semantic development into ‘movement/action’ remain unresolved.

The identification of bronze 童 and 動 as the same graph is a database’s paleographic account. The inspected evidence does not demonstrate a dated transitional chain from that graph to seal 動, or prove that 力 and 重 were already separable components in the bronze form.

The ‘person carrying a bag/load’ interpretation of early 重 is an external database’s analysis. Whether the depicted object was specifically a bag and what its spoken name was are not independently established here. This uncertainty does not undermine the attested phonetic role of 重 in received 動.

The cited early textual examples are given by source and locus, but no absolute composition or manuscript dates were established for each; no chronology is inferred from the dictionary’s ordered list of senses.
No evidence was found for a whole-graph phonetic loan in 動. The sound component 重 is treated separately from any hypothetical borrowing of a word for a depicted object.

The 1956 standardization table proves 动（動） as the simplified/traditional mapping, but the inspected sources do not establish whether 动 descends from an earlier cursive or popular variant; the cloud-like shape alone is insufficient to assign such ancestry.
Pronunciations reported in the local dossier for Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese and Tang readings were not independently checked in this external research.
No glyph pixels were visually inspected. The Commons files are proposed candidates based on their source descriptions; captions should be checked against the downloaded images before final selection.
The Commons bronze-file page could not be opened directly in this session; its metadata was available in a search result, so reuse terms and image identity need confirmation on the file page.
No individual Xiaoxuetang glyph record or official rights notice was successfully inspected; no Xiaoxuetang image is proposed.
The inspected sources do not establish an oracle-bone attestation, an absolute date for the earliest 動 graph, or a dated chain connecting a bronze form to received 動.
The reported identification of a bronze form as 童=動 is not independently verified in this session, and the early graph’s referent and semantic path to ‘action/movement’ remain unresolved.

Shuowen’s account supports the received form’s analysis but is a historical lexicographic claim, not independent proof of earlier graph history. The dossier’s suggested bronze-to-seal component history remains uncertain; do not classify the earlier graph as an ancestor or variant of 重 without further evidence.

CUHK cites early textual and manuscript uses but the inspected entry does not provide composition or manuscript dates sufficient to date the semantic extensions. No chronology is inferred from the order of glosses.

The source’s ‘person carrying a bag/load’ reading of 重 is not independent evidence for the depicted object’s original name or pronunciation. That name is not needed to support the received compound’s reported phonetic analysis, but its sound relation could not be independently checked against Baxter–Sagart because the PDF access failed.
The simplified form is officially paired with 動 in 1956; the browsed sources do not establish whether its graphic shape descends from an older cursive or popular variant.

The dossier’s Baxter–Sagart reconstruction comparison was not reverified because the source endpoint was inaccessible. Modern Mandarin readings were observed in CUHK; other language readings in the dossier were not independently checked.

items.period: Bronze-script style; source image reference B19049. The file description does not give an artifact date for this redraw.
items.tradition: Chinese bronze script, modern vector redraw
items.caption: This bronze-style rendering has an upper form with a separate short stroke above it and a lower enclosing form. Its identification as an early graph for 動 is reported in the paleographic record, but the graph’s original referent and its relation to the received form remain uncertain.
items.alt: Black bronze-script-style glyph with a short detached stroke above a large upper form and a lower rounded enclosure containing a small mark.
items.selection_reason: It provides a candidate early graphic form relevant to the record’s reported bronze-script identification, while its uncertain identification and historical relationship are stated explicitly.
items.rights: Commons labels the SVG public domain but also notes permission and copyright from Richard Sears’s site; confirm the specific file terms and any attribution before reuse.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; modern redraw of a historical script form, with no artifact date claimed.
items.tradition: Small-seal / Shuowen seal style, modern vector redraw
items.caption: In this seal-style rendering, the received form’s 力 and 重 components are visually distinguishable, illustrating the traditional lexicographic analysis of 動 as meaning-bearing 力 with 重 as phonetic.
items.alt: Black seal-script-style character with a complex upper section, a rounded middle enclosure, and a short base stroke.
items.selection_reason: It makes the documented received-form component analysis visible and complements the candidate bronze-style graph without asserting a direct chronological transition.
items.rights: Commons labels the vector representation public domain; attribution is appreciated but not required according to the file page.

limitations.text: The bronze-style graph’s identification and original referent are unresolved, and the available evidence does not establish a dated chain linking it to the received form.
The seal-style image is a modern redraw of a historical script style; it illustrates a lexicographic analysis rather than independently proving the graph’s earlier history.
